Recent findings suggest that I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.

YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.

More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to owners and adding more controls over the commentary.

These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.

After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:.

“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”.

It has been revealed that what a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.

In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.

According to recent reports, curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding latest voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.

Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.

Recent findings suggest that spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.

In a recent development, although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the company’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The university will conduct a series of measures after a former student was gang-raped at a fraternity house two years ago.

Cornell University is set to announce a “full review” of fraternities and sororities determining their future on campus after an alleged sexual assault there has brought scrutiny to the system at the Ivy League school.

University president Michael Kotlikoff unveiled the review on Monday in an patch outlining several steps the institution has taken after a woman mentioned she was gang raped at an on-campus fraternity’s house.

Cornell had already banned fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year after the gang-rape was alleged in a civil lawsuit that captured international attention.

“I know many in our community have lost confidence in the Cornell administration’s ability to prevent and respond to sexual violence,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter published on Monday. “You have raised necessary questions about what the administration is doing to keep our students safe and where we have fallen short.

“You have called for greater transparency and better communication about what we are doing so that nothing like this can ever happen at Cornell again. I am committed to doing the necessary work to rebuild that confidence: regularly communicating and engaging about the work we have been doing and will do to build a culture of care and responsibility.”.

The changes include re-evaluating policies towards drugs and alcohol on campus, programming changes in sexual assault and bystander intervention trainings, and hiring a newly introduced victim advocate to work in the school’s Sexual Harassment and Assault Response & Education (Share) office.

Kotlikoff’s letter came months after a woman named Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against several members of an on-campus fraternity who she said raped her after she was drugged in November of 2024. She filed a complaint with Cornell and the university police, but no criminal charges were filed.

It has been revealed that two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled in connection with the case. The others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.

All deny wrongdoing, while Jane Doe has expressed feeling unsupported and disbelieved by Kotlikoff.

Newly introduced York attorney general Letitia James is now conducting an investigation into the case.

Cornell was also scheduled to hold a community meeting on Monday evening, followed by two follow-up “listening sessions” for campus community members and staff in the coming weeks.

“These will be opportunities for open, frank, face-to-face conversations – and for advancing the work we can only do together,” Kotlikoff wrote in a note.

In early October, Cornell tapped Sally Yates, a former high-ranking US justice department official, to review the school’s policies around sexual assault.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.
  • It has been revealed that for starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there.
  • That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

It has been revealed that for starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, remarked in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, mentioned that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”.

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Sources indicate that alex Marshall is a Times reporter covering European culture. He is based in London.

Francesca Regalado is a Times reporter covering breaking news.

#331. Industry News: A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine demonstrates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1464 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine demonstrates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, indicates study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler noted.

Sources indicate that mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The latest nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

According to recent reports, the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

Sources indicate that “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler stated.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

According to recent reports, “They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an upgrade.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland remarked. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

Industry observers note that in reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

Industry observers note that “That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax claims it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in Upcoming York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a organization called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very key in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler stated.

Sources indicate that they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

Industry observers note that fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

According to recent reports, another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler mentioned, so it would have to be used carefully.

  • Industry observers note that they're not quite available on Apple TV yet, as according to the news outlet, early access is only for testing with developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple is finally adding video podcasts to Apple TV in a move that trails after major rivals like YouTube and Spotify.

First reported by The Upcoming York Times on Monday, the tech giant is testing video podcasts on its streaming platform. This means if your favourite show has a filmed element (which most major podcasts right now do), you'll be able to watch it in the same spot you mainline Apple Originals like Silo and Ted Lasso.

Industry observers note that they're not quite available on Apple TV yet, as according to the news outlet, early access is only for testing with developers. However, the NYT reports that video podcasts will be available soon and free for all, even if you don't have an Apple TV subscription.

Despite leading the podcast charge in 2005 and dominating listener stats, Apple has left eyeballs on the table when it comes to video podcasts — and not just because they're celebrity magnets and dynamite for clipped viral social media moments. Notably, the manufacturer did add video to its Podcast app in February, with the NYT reporting a 20 percent audience growth for top shows.

With video podcasts, Apple is contending with the behemoth that is YouTube, which has more than 1 billion monthly active podcast viewers. In April 2026, YouTube reported that Premium users watched over 800 million hours of podcasts.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, as of 2026, over 500 million consumers have streamed a video podcast on Spotify, an increase of 50 percent year over year, according to the firm. Like YouTube, Spotify is aware of the impact videos can have on growing podcast audiences. During its May 2026 Investor Day, Spotify also mentioned, "These users engage more, use more devices, and spend more time across podcasts, music, and audiobooks.".

Recent findings suggest that adding a podcast section to Apple TV will inevitably increase viewership for these reveals, which is great news for creators as much as Apple. However, not every podcast has a luxurious budget, celebrity hosts, and a polished studio, both of which are becoming increasingly crucial in the incessant battle for views.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
  • Sources indicate that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct.
  • The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Sources indicate that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, noted the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private organization.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

According to recent reports, foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the tech giant, which Pathak has noted is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

It has been revealed that the firm has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak mentioned in an April television interview.

It has been revealed that that April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump mentioned in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands.".

Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

Industry observers note that "Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren mentioned in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight.".

Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts.".

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, mentioned a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc noted at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

It has been revealed that insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, remarked the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the manufacturer's financial disclosures, the people said.

"This is what happens in a firm with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?".

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the manufacturer secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people remarked.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The manufacturer was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, stated as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

It has been revealed that federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job.".

#325. Industry News: The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

📅 03 Jan 2024 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-fresh planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that the world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand.
  • After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-fresh planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

Recent findings suggest that the world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the newly introduced year.

According to recent reports, if you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

It has been revealed that the undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

According to recent reports, the covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

Amazon (Techo, January 2027 Start).

Amazon (Cousin, January 2027 Start).

In a recent development, if you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

Shop (Single Notebook, A5 Slim).

Shop (Clear Vinyl Cover, A5 Slim).

Shop (Travel Notebook Set, A5 Alim).

According to recent reports, I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

Industry observers note that I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely latest planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

Recent findings suggest that I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and notable things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the initiative for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

Erin Condren (Academic Planner).

In a recent development, I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

Sources indicate that I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the upcoming year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most key to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”.

According to recent reports, academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the upcoming year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Industry observers note that like I remarked, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

Recent findings suggest that the Kokuyo Jibun Techo is another Japanese planner, but this one is a travel-notebook-style design, making it more customizable with a cover and multiple books that fit inside it. The First Kit comes with three books that fit into the included cover: Diary (labeled simply with the year), Life, and Idea. The 2026 versions are sold out, but you can buy the 2027 versions right now.

Looking for more of a monthly planner? The Big A## Planner is a massive planner with a nice monthly spread you can literally spread across your desk, with plenty of writing space for each day. Best for working from home, though; you don't want to have to fit this into your work bag.

If you're looking for a great daily planner, the Day Designer is a popular option for a reason. It's bulky since it has pages for every single day, but it leaves room for both your schedule and a long to-do list.

Plum Paper (A5 Vertical Priorities).

Plum Paper is my favorite classic-style planner, and you can easily customize it to start at any time of year and design the pages to fit your needs. I especially like the weekly A5 Vertical Priorities layout, and you can add all kinds of customizations into the daily columns, the habit tracker, and more to make it exactly what you want. But I've also left the habit tracker blank so I can adjust my habits as needed all year long.

Industry observers note that I bought this no-frills hardback during Prime Day last year, figuring I couldn’t go wrong for less than 20 bucks, and I was right. It’s a handy A5 size with a monthly view calendar at the beginning of each month, and then a 5-by-2.5-inch square for each day. That’s it. There are some plain lined pages in the back if you need more space for notes, but if your planning consists only of to-do lists and tracking deadlines, you will love this.—Kat Merck.

Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

In a recent development, ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

Industry observers note that laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

According to recent reports, leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

Recent findings suggest that papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

In a recent development, passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

In a recent development, looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

Industry observers note that passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson.

Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

Recent findings suggest that one of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

In a recent development, paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to blueprint out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

What Sizes Do Planners Come In?

It has been revealed that here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back up, finally ending its lengthy outage after over two weeks.
  • Industry observers note that non-profit parent organisation the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) announced AO3's triumphant return on Sunday, Nov.
  • Now AO3 has woken up, and while some features have been temporarily disabled to get the website back up more promptly, OTW states that no data was lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back up, finally ending its lengthy outage after over two weeks. The Hugo Award-winning fanfiction website went down due to a security incident late last month, and was expected to take up to four weeks to return. Fortunately it didn't take quite so long, with customers now taking to social media to celebrate AO3's revival.

Industry observers note that non-profit parent organisation the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) announced AO3's triumphant return on Sunday, Nov. 15 at 3:00 a.m. ET / 12:00 a.m. PT, almost exactly 17 days since it first confirmed the outage on Oct. 29 at 3:13 a.m. ET / 12:13 PT. This was also a mere day after the website turned 17, customers having lamented that AO3 spent its birthday "in a coma.".

Now AO3 has woken up, and while some features have been temporarily disabled to get the website back up more promptly, OTW states that no data was lost.

"Your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe," OTW noted in its update announcing AO3's return.

AO3's return is exciting news for millions of people. The internet went through a multi-fandom meltdown during the AO3 outage, which Forbes previously described as "the gold standard of fanfiction sites." Fanfiction-deprived fans took to sharing saved stories among themselves, while some even flocked to Tumblr for their fandom fix.

As such, the news of AO3's recovery swiftly spread, with some fanfiction readers rushing to spread the word on social media like Paul Revere on his midnight ride.

While many in the U.S. woke up to the news of AO3's recovery, others found out while otherwise going about their day. Attendees of a Yves concert in Melbourne, Australia learned of the development after X user @Alyssa_Aroha held up her phone in the crowd to display the words, "AO3 IS BACK UP." Video of this has since gone viral, racking up over 1.1 million views on X, with attendees reportedly having screamed and cheered at the news.

It has been revealed that not everybody at the K-pop concert understood the significance of @Alyssa_Aroha's message. Concertgoer and X user @gyublickyy noted that "the dude behind me was a self proclaimed 'the only straight person in a yves concert' and he was going what the hell is ao3." But for many others it was a moment of collective joy and community.

It has been revealed that "In the Yves concert, waiting for it to start, and people start screaming so I assume she's come out early," posted @himejoshiorbit. "No. AO3 is back.".

Meanwhile, attendees at Filipino komiks and art market PasKomiket reportedly learned of AO3's return from organisers who revealed it over their PA system. The news prompted cheers from the crowd, many of whom immediately attempted to access the website on their phones.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, fans have largely been understanding and patient, with many simply happy that AO3 is back. OTW has stated that its volunteers are continuing to work on restoring AO3's functionality, and will provide further updates as they come.

In a recent development, AO3 celebrated 11 million registered people in June, though it's likely that an even higher number of people missed it while it was down. AO3 only requires registration for publishing fanfiction, not reading it, OTW having reported that AO3 received an average of around 108 million daily page views in 2025.

According to recent reports, amanda Yeo is an Assistant Editor at Mashable, covering entertainment, culture, tech, science, and social good. Based in Australia, she writes about everything from video games and K-pop to movies and gadgets.

#319. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1680 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report demonstrates.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an vital purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report demonstrates. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an vital purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

Industry observers note that there is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the firm released and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

According to recent reports, “Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

According to recent reports, “We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

In a recent development, most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

Recent findings suggest that the cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

Recent findings suggest that and only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

In a recent development, many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

Recent findings suggest that “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

In a recent development, however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply concerns posed a challenge, forcing it to right now aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

Industry observers note that “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

According to recent reports, beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

In a recent development, “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” noted Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

In a recent development, sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

Industry observers note that the gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a manufacturer on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high reveals the scale of India's climate challenge.

“I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann remarked. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, claims the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability challenges) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”.

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

Chase Bank’s services are experiencing a technical bug matter, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson stated on Monday.

A spokesperson from US Bank said its systems are not directly affected; however, “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”.

Zelle’s network operator is a tech giant called Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.

Industry observers note that some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Drawquarium is the anti-AI cozy game that lets you create your own fish tank

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Who knew one of the most delightful responses to the incessant wave of AI slop would be a DIY fish tank game?
  • Developed by Kaleb Lechowski aka byKaleb, Drawquarium is a sweet upcoming cozy sandbox game out on Steam that's essentially the bloomscrolling of video games.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who knew one of the most delightful responses to the incessant wave of AI slop would be a DIY fish tank game?

Developed by Kaleb Lechowski aka byKaleb, Drawquarium is a sweet upcoming cozy sandbox game out on Steam that's essentially the bloomscrolling of video games. Since the trailer dropped, the game's been dubbed "anti-AI" and has seen commenters on YouTube and X delighted with the game's handcrafted feel — the "brb crying because of a fish game trailer" responses are accurate.

And according to the Lechowski's Steam description, the game is not for you if you "want action or excitement. No combat, no explosions. Think of Drawquarium as the opposite of GTA 😄.".

The premise of Drawquarium is simple: draw a fish, name it, and watch it come to life swimming in your own digital aquarium. The game is focused on unlocking your creativity and sense of lighthearted tomfoolery, as you can either use templates or come up with your own ungodly creations. Reader, I'm loving my octopus sick:.

Sources indicate that in his Steam notes, Lechowski describes why he, a 3D artist in the film industry, made Drawquarium: "My heart kept pulling me toward a small, very personal game idea. One of the reasons I started developing this game was that I wanted to bring my children’s drawings to life 💖." Can't argue with that.

It has been revealed that first, you'll need to title your aquarium, then it's time to draw your first fish and name them. I tend toward themes for sandbox games — shout out to my Gilmore Girls-themed faction in Cult of the Lamb — so I've named my creatures after sea goddesses.

Drawquarium's easel mode feels like a supercharged, thoughtful, fun version of MS Paint, with advanced digital brushes and tools that easily help you craft a fish-like being — and reader, when you accidentally fill the screen with the Paint Bucket instead of one section, there's an undo button. Drawing my first fish, I took more time than I thought, adding stripes and fins and flourishes to my little Amphitrite. Once you're happy with your undersea creature, click "give me my fish" and you'll drop your little creation into the tank.

Watching your work – be it a marine masterpiece or a passable abstract – swim around the tank is deeply satisfying. The fish spawn as tiny wee sea bairns and grow in size (something you can also set).

Industry observers note that once your fish is settled, you're instantly prompted to draw them a friend, which takes you back to the creative drawing board. You can clone the fish, start again, or if you need an idea, the lightbulb at the top of the easel will give you suggestions like "draw a steampunk fish," or "draw a fish reading the newspaper." You can unlock templates as you go, and the various photo editing tools you're used to are here: clone and replicate, mirroring, and erasing.

Recent findings suggest that of course, this is a drawing game, so you don't have to contain your creativity to sea creatures like I did (but my turtle slaps). Maybe your fish look like hats, stereos, or butts, all swimming in your own cursed little fish bowl. You do you, buttfish.

Decorating your tank with plants is next, as you can sketch out plants of a wild and wonderful nature. My one tip here is to play with the opacity and brush size settings, as you can create some satisfying tendrils of varying texture. And in a sweet feature, when it comes time to feed your fish with a click, it's also up to you to draw their meal. I know it's not ideal to feed octopus babies cupcakes but this is my aquarium, my choice of fish food.

You'll need to clean the tank floor (the fish instinctively run from the vacuum), and you can gather coins from the tank to buy more templates — at this stage, the game doesn't have real in-game transactions.

Once you've become thoroughly locked in to making new types of deep sea residents, there's a wallpaper mode which pops your aquarium onto your desktop so you can sit with your creations all day. This is the real magic of the game, bringing your painstakingly crafted (or slapdash) efforts into your everyday routine.

In week after week, month after month, of news about how AI is eating creatives' lunch, Drawquarium is a quietly triumphant achievement. A stunning use of human creativity in a deeply relaxing, cosy sandbox game, it's a refreshing treat.

Drawquarium is out on Steam (and as Creative Bloq points out, make sure you're buying the official game, as copies have popped up).

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

A Tomatometer-approved critic, Shannon writes about entertainment, tech, social good, science, culture, and Australian horror, and loves to nerd out with movie stars, filmmakers, and TV creators.

  • A three-in-one travel charger that can power up my iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods is one of the first items I pack for any trip.
