📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A three-in-one travel charger that can power up my iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods is one of the first items I pack for any trip. I’ve tried out plenty of options, but these are my favorite chargers for keeping the holy trinity of Apple gadgets going strong while on vacation or a work trip.

Many of these picks will also happily charge Qi2 Android phones and other devices that support wireless charging. Since space is at a premium when traveling, they all feature clever compact designs. I’ve also included two-in-one options if you want to travel even lighter.

If you want something for your desk or nightstand when you’re back home, check out our Best Apple 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Stations and Best Wireless Chargers guides, and for power on the go, read our Best Travel Adapters, Best Power Banks, and Best MagSafe Power Banks guides.

Updated November 2026: I added chargers from Peak Design and Mophie, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

Industry observers note that A classy look elevates this folding three-in-one stand charger, which accommodates your phone in portrait or landscape orientation. It is Qi2 25W-certified, so it can deliver 25 watts to supported phones (15 watts to others). There’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger on the back to fast-charge Apple Watch (Series 7 and above), and a spot for earbuds on the base. It feels sturdy and secure, with rubber grips to prevent sliding, and supports StandBy mode. It’s relatively compact for travel, but also looks good enough to be your permanent bedside charger. Not only does the whole thing fold flat, but it also comes with UK and EU adapters for the included power brick.

Satechi’s latest model is plastic with a soft-touch finish; the original version ($130) was more luxurious, with vegan leather and aluminum. The original is still a great option if you don’t mind the 15-watt charging rate.

In a recent development, packing space is often limited when you travel, so it’s very handy that Anker’s MagGo folds down to a slim, compact form. Despite the small size, it packs plenty of power, charging your iPhone or Qi2-certified phone at up to 15 watts on a magnetic pad that you can adjust to your preferred angle. A second pad behind the main one charges AirPods or other wireless earbuds, and there’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger.

It can feel a little crowded when fully loaded, but I appreciate the space-saving design when packing it in a bag. While you can find faster options with chargers that support Qi2 25W, they’re not widely available and make little difference if you charge your devices overnight.

Sources indicate that this cute, compact charging kit comes in a soft faux-leather bag. Unzip it to find a folding charger with a tiltable pad for your iPhone, a pad underneath for your AirPods, and a pop-up Apple Watch charger to the side. It comes with a 5-foot USB-C cable and a power adapter with fold-out prongs and three plug attachments (EU, UK, and AU). Everything is color-matched in black or cream, unless you opt for the special edition in orange and teal.

Sources indicate that ESR’s folding charger delivers 25-watt charging for Qi2 25W-supported phones, fast Apple Watch charging, and an effective cooling fan. This three-in-one model folds away neatly and has a strong magnetic pad that supports portrait or landscape orientation. You can also adjust the angles for the phone and watch chargers. The fan is relatively quiet, but I prefer total silence at night, so I was pleased to find a button that turns it off for when you’re trying to sleep.

It has been revealed that the plastic construction doesn’t feel premium, but it is lightweight, and the rubber feet do a decent job of preventing it from sliding around. It is more expensive than ESR’s previous release, the HaloLock, and the faster charging probably isn’t worth it if you’re primarily charging overnight, but overall it is a decent travel charger with a speed boost.

According to recent reports, with a clean white finish, an elegant folding design, and warm ambient light, this Journey charger is a delightful travel companion. Ordinarily, I hate superfluous lights on a charger, but this isn’t a pointless LED; it’s a gentle glow from behind the Apple Watch shelf on the back, with a touch-sensitive power button on the front. It’s nice to have when you wake up in an unfamiliar, pitch-dark hotel room. You can fold it out to stand mode to charge all three Apple gadgets at once, or lay it flat if you just need to charge your iPhone and AirPods.

In a recent development, while this folding charger isn’t quite as compact as Anker’s below, I love that you can use the iPhone charging pad when it’s folded up. The Apple Watch charger can also pop up for Nightstand mode. It’s finished in a soft faux leather and folds flat for easy carrying in the included pouch. You get a cable to plug into the USB-C port, but no power supply, so you’ll need to provide a 30-watt power adapter. There is also a two-in-one version ($80) for just your iPhone and Apple Watch.

If you are really pressed for space, this is the smallest three-in-one charger you can get. It folds up to resemble a macaron and is easy to stow, but it’s not a power bank, so you do still need a cable and wall charger (both supplied). Unfolded, you get a magnetic pad to charge your iPhone at up to 15 watts, a middle pad for your AirPods, and an Apple Watch charger on the right. The design is lovely to handle, with a soft-touch finish and a durable silicone strap. I still prefer stand-style chargers because they allow you to angle your iPhone and use StandBy mode, but the MagGo UFO lets you travel as light as possible.

More stylish and compact than the other options listed here, this two-in-one charger from Peak Design folds flat for easy stowing. Open it to reveal a base with a channel for a USB-C cable and a Qi2 25W charging pad, plus a second swiveling Qi2 25W pad on top. You can charge two phones, or a phone and wireless earbuds. There’s also a USB-C port on the side, so you can plug in a third device, or a watch or ring charger. It comes with a cable, but you’ll need a power adapter (45-watt minimum). I like Peak Design’s 65W Dual Slim Charger ($65), but you don’t have to spend that much.

This genius petite gadget is perfect for folks who love to travel light. It’s an Apple Watch charger with a handy carabiner you can clip to your key ring or bag strap. Rotate the magnetic pad, and a USB-C jack pops out. Just to be clear, this is not a power bank—you must plug it into your MacBook, a USB-C port on a wall adapter, or even your iPhone to charge your Apple Watch. It doesn’t get more portable than this.

UAG 3-in-1 Travel and Desktop Charger.

Industry observers note that UAG SRGE 3-in-1 Travel and Desktop Charger for $100: This charger was close to earning a top spot until I saw the price (regularly $165). It’s a very smart charging kit that folds flat and comes in a snazzy zip-up bag with a 4-foot braided USB-C cable and a 25-watt power adapter, including plugs for the US, UK, and Europe. You can prop your iPhone at different angles on the MagSafe stand, and it works well with StandBy mode and Nightstand mode for your Apple Watch, but it’s not Qi2-certified, so you won’t get the stated 15-watt charging for an iPhone.

Mophie 3-in-1 Travel Charger With MagSafe for $150: This little travel kit is the older version of our pick above, but it’s still good (especially if you find it on sale). It also comes with a carrying case, charging brick, and USB-C cable. The square stack unfolds to reveal three wireless chargers in one elongated pad. The iPhone sticks magnetically to the center (15 watts), and the Apple Watch dock supports Nightstand mode. There’s also a grooved spot for the AirPods. It works well and is pretty lightweight and compact.

Twelve South Butterfly Travel 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $80: This uber-compact two-in-one charger looks like a hockey puck. Open the Butterfly, and you’ll find two pads attached with a rubbery silicone material. You can fast-charge an Apple Watch on one—even popping the charger up to take advantage of Nightstand mode—and the other circle lets you recharge your MagSafe iPhone at 15 watts. It’s a super compact solution, and Twelve South includes a 30-watt power source and cable with international plug adapters.

Native Union Voyage 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $100: For a slightly lower price, former WIRED reviews editor Adrienne So likes Native Union’s Qi2 butterfly solution, which doesn’t include plug adapters but comes in a tidy travel pouch and includes a cable.

Kuxiu Qi2 25W Travel Charging Station: This charger folds down to an impressively small package, and it feels sturdy with a silicone-covered metal construction. It can hit 25 watts for supported Qi2 25W phones, comes in a few different finishes, and ships with a 45-watt power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. Unfortunately, I don’t like how it looks, and I found it awkward to charge all three devices at once. It’s actually so compact that it feels crowded.

Mous Travel Charger: While the compact, folding design and low price impressed me, it gets kinda warm when you charge all three of your Apple devices, and the AirPods spot is finicky.

Sources indicate that most of my picks are MagSafe or Qi2-certified wireless chargers. That means they take advantage of the magnets embedded in the back of the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 ranges. The magnets ensure perfect alignment, enabling faster and more efficient wireless charging.

Sources indicate that qi2 is a wireless charging standard that Apple worked with the Wireless Power Consortium to develop. Compared to the original Qi standard, it brings MagSafe-style magnetic charging, enabling faster charging rates and improved efficiency. Apple updated the iPhone 12 and newer to support Qi2, but it’s not just for Apple phones; other phones can get Qi2 certification. While Qi2 Android phones are still thin on the ground, you’ll find Qi2 in Google's Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series, and there are Qi2-ready phones that add magnets via a compatible case.

Qi2 charging mostly goes up to 15 watts, but the Qi2.2 update, branded as Qi2 25W, goes up to 25 watts. Support for Qi2 25W is presently limited and includes the iPhone 17 and 18 range and the Pixel 10 Pro XL and Pixel 11 range.

Sources indicate that if you use a case, make sure it is MagSafe- or Qi2-compatible. A normal case will weaken the pull of the magnets in the device and will not stick to chargers as well. If your case is too thick, your phone may not charge at all.

MagSafe is also available in the AirPods charging case (depending on your model). Apple’s AirPods and AirPods Pro with the wireless charging case work with nearly all standard Qi wireless charging pads (as do many third-party wireless earbuds), but if you have AirPods with MagSafe, you can also connect them to magnetic mounts.

What Are StandBy and Nightstand Modes?

I mention StandBy and Nightstand modes throughout this guide, but what are they?

StandBy mode was introduced in iOS 17. When you place your iPhone on a charger in landscape orientation, it turns the screen into a smart display to show the time (with different clock designs to choose from), photos from your library, or widgets. If your iPhone supports an always-on screen, you can set it to turn off automatically after a set time when the iPhone isn't in use or when the room is dark. Head to Settings > Standby to customize it.

It has been revealed that nightstand mode highlights the time on your Apple Watch when it’s sitting upright and charging, so it can serve as a bedside clock. You can customize this on your Apple Watch by heading to Settings > General > Nightstand mode.

  • That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers remarked they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

"We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

In a recent development, EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

In a recent development, legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that.

"We try not to proposal for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe said Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done.".

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

"You know, they say, 'Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it.".

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

CNBC previously reported that House Democrats proposal to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, mentioned she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

"I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, said. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for.".

Scout's Keogh mentioned if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

"I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh said. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer.".

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Cox Automotive reports the average price for a upcoming electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

In a recent development, "Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, mentioned Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, noted on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.
  • The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec.
  • South Sudan has never held a national election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, noted on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.

The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process.

South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.

Recent findings suggest that in 2013, civil war broke out between the government and forces loyal to the main opposition leader, Riek Machar. Under a peace agreement to end the conflict in 2018, Mr. Machar became the vice president in a transitional government.

Industry observers note that the upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

According to recent reports, with Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

Sources indicate that the election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

Recent findings suggest that “The conditions for credible polls are not right now in place,” the International Crisis Group said in a briefing for the U.N. Security Council this week. “Rushed elections could be a decisive final blow to the 2018 framework and would open the door to a return to sustained large-scale violence.”.

It has been revealed that mr. Ateny, the information minister, acknowledged that the government could not gain access to “small parts” of the country, but remarked the election would be credible.

“It’s not always 100 percent, but it can be good for the sovereignty of the country and it’s good for the mandate of the state,” he noted in an interview.

In addition to the violence and civil unrest, South Sudanese have been faced with soaring food prices, drought and flooding. Of the country’s roughly 12 million people, more than 8 million are in need of food assistance, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a globally recognized monitor of hunger.

Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity.

Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.

Industry observers note that the office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections , and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives mentioned.

According to recent reports, the disruption began Thursday with US users reporting interrupted access to their Outlook email accounts. As it continued into the next day, millions of people worldwide said they could not access their email in any capacity as well as other Office 365 services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The firm did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach.

In a post on X on Monday, Charles Lamanna, the executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said there was a latent bug or defect from July that caused Microsoft’s servers to “become overwhelmed and unresponsive”.

Lamanna wrote that the company typically has two available networking gateways, or entry and exit points that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them. However, one of them was not working for Microsoft Teams which overwhelmed the primary gateway. Subsequently, over 14% of the company’s server capacity was also not working due to an unrelated problem from the previous day.

“Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna wrote. “This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States.”.

The company also had trouble mitigating the bug because it originated months before, Lamanna said, so it would not be easy as rolling back a recent change to undo the defect.

“Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” he wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to promptly revert the change.”.

The firm prepares to publish a final report which will include more information, he remarked.

Analysts say Microsoft’s global outage highlights the need for companies to examine how much they rely on a single operating system.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a prime example of the importance of not only cyber resilience, but business resilience,” said Matt Hull, vice-president of cyber intelligence and response at NCC Group. “Reports that hospitals, schools and other essential services are affected demonstrate the wide impact that a system outage can have, regardless of the cause.”.

#305. Tech Report: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1938 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million owners a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Industry observers note that multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders remarked the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

Industry observers note that the revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

According to recent reports, there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg noted a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly consumers until the end of 2018, the year it listed in Fresh York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the manufacturer set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they mentioned.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the firm was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting people to open the app and place orders, they mentioned.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

According to recent reports, google Play is not available in China, and Android people in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it stated it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen noted. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

Industry observers note that in China, about three quarters of smartphone people are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, remarked Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

Industry observers note that “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he stated.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

In a recent development, pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he remarked.

According to recent reports, according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews demonstrated that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Industry observers note that suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread promptly among other researchers, who did name the tech giant. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the enhancement, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

According to recent reports, the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the tech giant’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to massive data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source remarked.

Recent findings suggest that most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, mentioned although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

It has been revealed that “This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” mentioned Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

The FBI is leading the investigation into the Biourja Renewables incident after it led to a temporary evacuation.

Authorities investigating a bomb found recently at an ethanol production plant in Peoria, Illinois, have taken a suspect into custody, according to the mayor there.

The Peoria mayor, Rita Ali, told the Guardian on Monday that leadership at the BioUrja Renewables plant “have informed me that a suspect is in custody”.

Ali noted the FBI – which is leading the investigation into the bomb – is expected to release more details later.

In a separate statement on Monday, the FBI’s division in nearby Springfield, Illinois, announced that its agents “were conducting law enforcement activity … in connection with the Biourja Renewables explosives device incident”.

“The investigation remains ongoing,” said the FBI, which added that it was receiving assistance from the federal bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Illinois state police, the local sheriff’s office, the Peoria police department and the police department of adjacent East Peoria.

The Guardian has contacted the FBI for additional comment.

Ali’s comments came after her administration ordered thousands of residents in parts of Peoria to evacuate their homes and businesses because authorities discovered an explosive device at BioUrja Renewables.

According to recent reports, the ethanol for fuel and alcohol which the plant produces is highly flammable. And the riverfront facility spans an area that is roughly equivalent to 44.5 US football fields.

The Peoria police chief, Brad Dixon, remarked a potential explosion could have affected an area within a one-mile radius – but that technicians had rendered the bomb safe.

The evacuation zone ordered by local authorities encompassed a part of East Peoria, which is a separate municipality. Local events were canceled as streets in the affected area were closed to the public.

It has been revealed that officials lifted the evacuation order at about 1.25pm on Saturday after they determined that no additional explosives had been found. They didn’t immediately announce any arrests but made clear they were working to identify any suspects in connection with the bomb.

Sources indicate that bomb threats and suspicious package calls are relatively common for law enforcement. Officials take those kinds of calls seriously as they investigate them. But they often aren’t verified as credible or substantial, making the case in Peoria – a city with about 110,000 residents – somewhat rare.

#301. Tech Report: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1204 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
  • But just as he’s leaving, the organization has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck.
  • “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI tech giant, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the organization has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI tech giant, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

According to recent reports, nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Industry observers note that major US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Sources indicate that several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a tech giant that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a firm that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more key. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead mentioned, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the manufacturer in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The tech giant’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other substantial market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

According to recent reports, huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

According to recent reports, huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, notes Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

According to recent reports, even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Sources indicate that most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead indicates the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

According to recent reports, but Moorhead indicates the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

In a recent development, every time a major upcoming open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he notes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.

He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.

Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.

Recent findings suggest that before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair stated.

Sources indicate that last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.

The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair remarked. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.

A man has appeared in court charged with causing the deaths of two people in a car crash in Leeds.

Leigh Ross, 39, was charged in connection with an incident in which Cameron Bell, 22, and Jade Langton, 23, were killed in the early hours of Sunday.

Ross, of Harrogate, wept in the dock as he made his first appearance in court on Monday, and his voice broke as he was asked to confirm his date of birth and address.

He is charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing death by driving a vehicle while uninsured, two counts of causing death by driving a vehicle while disqualified and two counts of causing death having taken a vehicle without consent.

Recent findings suggest that he was remanded in custody until his next appearance at Leeds crown court. As he was leaving the dock, he looked towards the public gallery and said: “I’m sorry.”.

West Yorkshire police stated a chase began at 12.44am on Sunday after a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road.

The vehicle then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco that was turning into Gelderd Road from Lowfields Road.

Sources indicate that bell, from York, who was driving the Volkswagen, died at the scene. His passenger, Langton, also from York, was pronounced dead in hospital a short time later.

In a recent development, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a girl, 16, were also arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. They have been released on bail pending further inquiries.

The West Yorkshire force has referred itself to the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which has introduced an investigation into the incident.

Detectives are appealing to anyone who saw the collision, or has dashcam, mobile phone or CCTV footage, to contact West Yorkshire police via 101 or online.

Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this holiday season, substantial-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs.
  • "We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these significant-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.
  • Weinswig remarked retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this holiday season, substantial-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these significant-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig remarked retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year.".

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Recent findings suggest that industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology firm OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.

In a recent development, UPS CEO Carol Tomé mentioned on the company's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers.".

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, noted retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers mentioned.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Firm's annual forecast. Leathers mentioned even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

According to recent reports, "The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers noted. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf.".

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding latest team members.

According to recent reports, "Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania remarked.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry.".

Amit Regev, CEO of drone organization Flytrex, remarked the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev said.

It has been revealed that retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September noted it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

Sources indicate that "Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev mentioned. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones.".

#292. How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis.
  • In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.
  • The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis.

In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.

Industry observers note that many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill.

That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable.

On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people.

Industry observers note that milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work.

In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line.

After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity.

Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them.

According to recent reports, “Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.”.

He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard.

Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead.

Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market.

Burnham has stated he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment.

His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”.

The massive difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term.

Recent findings suggest that the rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have.

His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs.

So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden mentioned: “What is proposed is a upcoming settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR.”.

The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

  • You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one.
  • Industry observers note that to answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

Industry observers note that to answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a newly introduced Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

This cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security tech giant Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

In a recent development, the 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

It has been revealed that birdbuddy's brand-new Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

Birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The upcoming Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

It has been revealed that camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

Industry observers note that I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

Birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is notable; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

It has been revealed that this feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the massive downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

Sources indicate that after experiencing connection issues with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

It has been revealed that there's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

Industry observers note that so far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.).

Sources indicate that I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.).

Birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

Wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

Kiwibit’s upcoming enhancement to its original Feeder 2 is an interesting one; it’s the first bird feeder camera to feature autofocus in 4K HDR. The quality was exceptional, though, during my testing, some birds were alarmed by the camera movement. The biggest downside, though, is that most of this feeder’s features—including AI bird identification, expanded gallery views, and 60-day cloud storage—are now locked behind a $90-a-year paywall. It's not enough of an upgrade to justify paying the extra cash over the base-model Bird Feeder 2.

A lower-maintenance way to enjoy birds in your yard, this recycled-plastic birdbath comes outfitted with a dual-lens camera sending 1080p photos and 2K video via the Birdfy app and using the app’s AI capability for (free) bird identification. With the IP66-rated birdbath’s sturdy metal base (you can buy it for less without) and solar-powered battery and fountain pump, all you have to do is make sure the 3.5-liter, 1.65-inch reservoir is topped off with water. I've been using the Bath Pro for two seasons now, and while early connection complications have been resolved, the plastic has weathered, and the pump only works intermittently. I also find myself increasingly irritated with how long footage takes to load and how often the shallow plastic basin needs refilling and cleaning—every two or three days in dry weather. Still, if you're willing to put up with some quirks, the Bath Pro has been an entertaining and welcome addition to my bird-feeding setup.
